beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, a section header

beats.trigger: The hard part is not access; it is absorption.
beats.got: Handing my team the tools won't be what decides whether they use them.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: I should have brought an example. I have one: the CRM rollout.

beats.trigger: **Name** the likely adoption failure before it happens, including the social failure that's hardest to see
beats.got: A list of five verbs. The failure-naming one is the useful one.

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: My hesitation is that my version only works because I fix its output every time.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not from my setup. It's fair, but it's the second time I've been told this.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The agent interviews against my files and I check whether the result is specific to one person. That works for me.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Choose the sharing form by the outcome, not by what's convenient. That's how I read vendor pitches already.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, a handoff to the next exercise

beats.trigger: find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it
beats.got: nothing new, setup for the next exercise

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Look for the one obstacle behind the others, not the first technical limit. For my team that is probably the missing shared place for context files.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: My people plan will be full of UNASSIGNED. That's the real status of my team's rollout, and I'd not seen it before.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: Treat the plans as hypotheses and test them. Consultants already do this.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: A sharp question for each teammate. It's the kind of question I'd ask in a strategy engagement.

beats.trigger: one person, one question about how they do the job today, and one selected assumption with its test.
beats.got: I leave with one named conversation and one test I can do next week. This is the part I came for.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: The sequence is job, then candidate, then plans, then test the switch. 'Shopping' is a good line.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of it.
beats.got: nothing new, a framing line

beats.trigger: The outcome sentence you wrote is the contract
beats.got: nothing new, this is the third time the job comes first

beats.got: The value is in the curation and the corrections, not in the prompt or agent file. So my fourteen people copying my instructions would get a generic answer.

take_homes: Don't share my agent. Share one of context, a skill, the output or an interface, picked by the job my teammate is doing, not by what's convenient for me.
Draft the people plan next to the technical plan. If the roles stay UNASSIGNED, that is where the rollout really stands.
Before I push anything at the team, ask what would have to be true for a person to drop their current way of working. Test one assumption with one named person.

monday.move: Pick one of the fourteen, probably whoever owns the pricing-pilot data. Ask how they do their part of the usage-pricing brief today, and test the assumption that they'd use the pilot-cohort brief if it landed where they already look. Also start writing the people plan to find who could own a shared place for context files.
monday.who: One teammate on the pricing working group, and the person who could own the shared context folder
monday.when: Monday, a 30-minute conversation, before the pricing working group meets
monday.stop_condition: If the teammate says they'd keep using their current spreadsheet or private copy, I stop pushing the candidate and redesign around what they said.
monday.blocker: There is still no shared place for context files and no named owner for it. Everyone keeps their own copy.

misconception.why: I thought getting good at this meant better prompts. The lecture said the value is in the curated memory and the corrections, and that passing on instructions gives people a generic answer. It didn't fully change my view, because I still think a sharper brief matters, but it's no longer the main thing.

one_line: The exercises were worth my time and left me with a named person and a test for Monday. The lecture said the same thing three times, so I'd cut it in half.
